title: Folk Music
objective: After this level you can explain how folk songs pass from person to person.
summary: Folk music lives in oral tradition, changing as it passes by ear. 'Barbara Allen', heard by Pepys in 1666, has so many versions the Library of Congress issued an LP of them.

cards.headline: In 1666, Samuel Pepys heard a song people kept singing for centuries.
cards.body: In January 1666, the London diarist Samuel Pepys wrote of the pleasure of hearing the actress Mrs. Knipp sing 'her little Scotch song of Barbary Allen.' Folklore collectors would later find 'Barbara Allen' more often than almost any other ballad. How does a song stay alive that long, and why does it never come out quite the same?

cards.headline: Folk songs travel by ear
cards.body: Britannica describes folk music as traditional, generally rural music passed down through families and other small social groups. It lives in oral tradition: people learn it by hearing rather than reading. And as a song passes along, it varies, reshaped by singers' creativity and by their forgetfulness. That's why a folk song rarely has one 'correct' version. Every singer is a little bit of an editor.

mascot.line: Forgot a verse and made one up? Congratulations, you're a folk singer.

cards.headline: Old songs in the Appalachian hills
cards.body: Between 1916 and 1918, the English collector Cecil Sharp and his assistant Maud Karpeles spent 46 weeks in the Southern Appalachian mountains. He collected songs straight from mountain singers: some of obvious English origin, others, like the square dance, distinctly American. The singers themselves were the archive.

cards.headline: One ballad, a whole album of versions
cards.body: 'Barbara Allen' is one of the ballads folklore fieldworkers have collected most often, under many names and in many versions. In 1966 the Library of Congress released an entire LP of it, Versions and Variants of the Tunes of Barbara Allen, edited by Charles Seeger from its Archive of Folk Song. Same sad story, many different tunes: oral tradition you can hear.

cards.headline: Folk music: passed on
learned: Folk songs live in oral tradition, learned by ear
Each singer's changes create new versions
Cecil Sharp found old songs in Appalachia
'Barbara Allen' filled a whole Library of Congress LP

questions.prompt: What did Samuel Pepys record in his diary in January 1666?

options.label: Hearing Mrs. Knipp sing 'her little Scotch song of Barbary Allen'
Printing the first songbook of English and Scottish ballads
options.rationale: Pepys wrote about hearing the song.

options.label: Meeting Cecil Sharp to collect ballads in Appalachia
Composing both the words and tune of 'Barbara Allen'
options.rationale: He heard it sung; he didn't write it.

questions.explanation: Pepys wrote of the pleasure of hearing Mrs. Knipp sing 'her little Scotch song of Barbary Allen.'

questions.prompt: Why do folk songs like 'Barbara Allen' exist in so many versions?

options.label: Publishers printed deliberately different editions
options.rationale: Folk music lives mainly in oral tradition, not print.

options.label: Every version was written by a different composer
options.rationale: The variants grew as the song was passed on.

options.label: Learned by ear, a song changes as each singer passes it on
Singers were required to change one verse
options.rationale: Change comes from creativity and forgetfulness, not rules.

questions.explanation: Folk songs are learned by hearing, and each singer's creativity or forgetfulness reshapes them.

questions.prompt: Level 54's griots and a ballad singer in the Appalachians have what in common?

options.label: Both accompany themselves on the 21-string kora
Both keep songs and history alive through oral tradition
Both learn their songs from printed scores and books
options.rationale: Both learn and pass on material by ear.

options.label: Both inherit the job from a hereditary family line
options.rationale: Griots are hereditary; folk singers generally aren't described that way.

questions.explanation: Griots preserve oral traditions, and folk songs live in oral tradition, passed on by hearing.
